1 INTRODUCTION
1.1 Purpose of this Report
This Report outlines the Authority’s review of the Uganda Electricity
Supply Industry (ESI) Main Grid Tariff for the Fourth Quarter of 2025
(October to December). It details the outcomes of the tariff
assessment and the approved revenue requirements that
informed the End-user Electricity Tariffs applicable for the period
October 2025 to December 2025.
1.2 Background
Following the takeover by Uganda Electricity Distribution
Company Limited (UEDCL) of the concession formerly operated
by Umeme Limited in April 2025, the Authority, at its 424th meeting,
considered and approved the revised 2025 Base Electricity Tariff,
taking into account the following:
(a) The consolidated operations of UEDCL;
(b) The approved Tariff Performance Parameters for UEDCL;
(c) Umeme Limited’s Buyout Amount; and
(d) The integration of energy sales, customer numbers, and
tariff reduction initiatives within the former Umeme
concession areas.
The Fourth Quarter of 2025 Tariff Review was conducted in
accordance with:
(a) UEDCL’s Licences for Distribution and Sale of Electricity;
(b) Uganda Electricity Generation Company Limited (UEGCL)’s
Licence for Generation and Sale of Electricity for Nalubaale
and Kiira Hydro Power Stations;
(c) The Bulk Power Supply Licence issued to Uganda Electricity
Transmission Company Limited (UETCL); and
(d) The Quarterly Tariff Adjustment Methodology, 2014.
In determining the Capacity Price for Nalubaale and Kiira Hydro
Power Stations, the Bulk Supply Tariff for UETCL, and the Distribution

1.4 Review Process – Stakeholder Consultations
As part of the Fourth Quarter 2025 Tariff Review process, the
Authority conducted stakeholder engagements to ensure
transparency and inclusivity. Key stakeholders consulted included
the Ministry of Energy and Mineral Development (MEMD), the
Uganda Manufacturers Association (UMA), and representatives
from the media. During these engagements, the Authority
provided detailed explanations about factors influencing the tariff
determination for the Fourth Quarter of 2025; particularly the
changes in macroeconomic indicators relative to the assumptions
used in the Base Tariff, and the need to ensure financial
sustainability of the ESI.

3 DEMAND ASSUMPTIONS
3.1 Maximum Demand
A review of system summaries reported by UETCL, covering the
period from January 2024 to July 2025, revealed a notable
increase in electricity demand. In July 2025, the system registered
a peak demand of approximately 1,287.43 MW, which included
exports of 42.17 MW to Tanzania, 94.60 MW to Kenya, and 81.16
MW to Rwanda. This maximum system demand occurred on 29th
July 2025, and represented an increase from 1,202.85 MW
recorded in June 2025.
The maximum domestic demand stood at approximately 1,069.50
MW, recorded during the peak period on 29th July 2025,
compared to 1,023.21 MW in June 2025. The shoulder peak system
demand was recorded at approximately 1,105.52 MW in July 2025,
up from 991.77 MW in June 2025. The off-peak maximum system
demand reached 877.03 MW in July 2025, compared to 812.28
MW in June 2025. The lowest system demand was recorded at
554.64 MW during the off-peak period on July 14, 2025, up from
527.40 MW in June 2025.
The July 2025 peak system demand of 1,287.43 MW represents a
27.83% increase compared to the 1,000.12 MW recorded in July
2024. This growth in demand is primarily attributed to increased
foreign direct investment in the mining and oil sectors, strategic
government interventions, expansion in agricultural production,
and the continued implementation of national programs such as
the Parish Development Model (PDM). Additionally, tariff reduction
and demand stimulation initiatives approved by the Authority
have contributed to the observed growth in electricity
consumption.

to Kenya, Tanzania, and Rwanda during the year, following the

3.2 Country's Economic Performance and Growth
According to the Bank of Uganda’s Monetary Policy Statement for
August 2025, the Central Bank Rate (CBR) was maintained at
9.75%. This decision aimed to support price stability while
promoting sustainable economic growth, particularly in light of
global uncertainties and heightened inflationary risks.

According to the Bank of Uganda, Uganda’s economy continues
to strengthen, with real GDP growth for the FY 2024/25 estimated
at 6.3% up from 6.1% in the previous fiscal year.
This growth is attributed to a recovery in household spending
driven by rising real incomes, improved agricultural and industrial
output, increased investment in the extractives sector, and the
continued implementation of government initiatives such as the
Parish Development Model (PDM). For the FY2025/26, overall
economic growth is projected to remain within the range of 6.0%
to 6.5%.
While growth prospects remain favourable, the Bank of Uganda
notes that downside risks persist. These include declining
commodity prices, global supply chain disruptions, tighter
financing conditions, and adverse weather patterns. However, the
economy could experience accelerated growth if geopolitical
tensions ease, infrastructure investments expand, and business
confidence improves. The medium-term outlook remains positive,
underpinned by strategic government initiatives and resilient
domestic activity.

4.2 Energy Purchases by UETCL from the Generation Power Plants
At the time of determining the 2025 Base Electricity Tariffs,
electricity demand was projected to grow at an annual rate of
approximately 10.4% compared to energy purchases in 2024. Total
energy purchases by UETCL were expected to increase from
6,622.85 GWh in 2024 to 7,311.6 GWh in 2025. For the Fourth
Quarter of 2025, annualised energy purchases are projected to
reach 8,241.24 GWh, representing a 24.44% increase compared to
2024.
This growth is attributed to the resilience of Uganda's economy in
the face of global economic pressures, including geopolitical
tensions and tighter monetary policy measures implemented by
the Central Bank, which helped cushion inflationary impacts.
Additional support for demand growth stems from the connection
of the West Nile region to the national grid, the rollout of the
Electricity Access Scale-Up Project, increased export opportunities
to Rwanda, Kenya, and Tanzania, and the commissioning of
transmission infrastructure that is expected to unlock suppressed
demand across the country. Furthermore, increased consumption
by industrial consumers has been stimulated by tariff reduction
initiatives approved by the Authority.
The projection of electricity consumption assumes stable global
economic conditions, with no major disruptions. This stability is
expected to support uninterrupted business operations, continued
easing of inflationary pressures, and overall economic growth
ranging between 6.5% and 7% over the next twelve months, as
projected by the Bank of Uganda. The positive outlook is further

4.2.1 Large Hydro Power Plants
(a) Nalubaale and Kiira Hydro Power Plants (380 MW)
The Nalubaale and Kiira Hydro Power Complex, with a combined
installed capacity of 380 MW, plays a central role in meeting
national electricity demand. The facility is operated by UEGCL,
which was issued a Licence for Generation and Sale of Electricity
for a period of three (3) years, effective April 2023, by the
Authority.
In Q4 2025 Tariff determination, the Kiira and Nalubaale Hydro
Power Plants are projected to be dispatched at an average
output of 211.74 MW, translating into an estimated energy
generation of 1,854.87 GWh. The dispatch levels from this hydro
complex are expected to influence the operational scheduling of
other power plants along the River Nile, due to the
interconnected nature of the river's hydrological regime.

(b) Bujagali Hydro Power Plant (250 MW)
In 2025, the Bujagali Hydro Power Plant is projected to operate at
an average capacity of 156.68 MW, resulting in an estimated
energy generation of 1,372.5 GWh. This generation level is
influenced by the regulated water release from the Kiira and
Nalubaale Hydro Power Complex, which has been limited to 1,000
cubic meters per second (Cumecs) by the Directorate of Water
Resource Management.
For the purpose of determining power purchase costs for Q4 2025,
the annualised dispatch from Bujagali Hydro Power Plant is
projected at 1,661.09 GWh. Consequently, the power purchase
costs for Bujagali Energy Limited are expected to decline from USh
445.3 billion in Q3 2025 to USh 435.62 billion in Q4 2025. This
reduction is primarily attributed to the appreciation of the Uganda
Shilling against the United States Dollar.
In July 2017, the Government of Uganda approved a five-year
waiver of Corporate Income Tax for Bujagali Energy Limited as a
tariff management measure aimed at reducing electricity costs.
That same year, the Government—through the Ministry of Finance,
Planning and Economic Development—committed to Bujagali
Energy Limited's lenders to extend the waiver for a period aligned
with the refinanced debt structure, spanning fifteen years. This
commitment formed part of the conditions for the debt
refinancing arrangement.

(c) Isimba Hydro Power Plant (183 MW)

However, the plant was expected to undergo major maintenance

In the determination of power purchase costs in the Fourth

The power purchase costs for Isimba Hydro Power Plant are

billion in Q4 2025. This projected decrease is attributed to the
appreciation of the Uganda Shilling against the United States

maintenance activities.

projected to generate at an average capacity of 101.54 MW,
resulting in an annualised energy output of approximately 889.51
GWh. This represents a decline from the 1,112 GWh generated in

According to the Licence issued for Karuma HPP, the plant is
contracted at an energy charge of US Cents 4.97 per kWh for the
first ten years following commissioning. This tariff is subject to
adjustment based on changes in the United States Producer Price
Index (US PPI). For the 2025 Tariff Year, the adjusted energy tariff

The annualised power purchase costs for Karuma Hydro Power
Plant are projected to decrease from USh 176.1 billion in Q3 2025

combined effect of lower dispatch levels and the appreciation of
the Uganda Shilling against the United States Dollar, which has
reduced the cost of dollar-denominated components in the tariff
structure.
(e) Achwa 1 and Achwa 2 Hydro Power Plants (87.2 MW)
The Agago Achwa Hydro Power Plant comprises two facilities:
Achwa 1, with an installed capacity of 46.2 MW, and Achwa 2,
with a capacity of 41 MW. Achwa 2 commenced commercial
operations in 2019, while Achwa 1 achieved commercial
operations in August 2021.
For the determination of power purchase costs in the Fourth
Quarter of 2025, the annualized dispatch from the Agago Achwa
complex is projected at 694.4 GWh.

10.1 Determination of The Adjustment Factors for the Fourth
Quarter of 2025
10.1.1 Foreign Exchange Rate Adjustment Factor (FERAF)
Movements in the exchange rate of the Uganda Shilling against
major currencies directly affect ESI costs, as significant
expenditures are denominated in foreign currency while tariffs
and revenues are collected in Uganda Shillings.
Between February 2025 and August 29, 2025, the Shilling
appreciated by 3.47% against the US Dollar, from USh 3,679.73/USD
to USh 3,552.1/USD. This appreciation reduced the Uganda Shilling
equivalent of the costs incurred in foreign currency.
10.1.2 Inflation Rate Adjustment Factor (IRAF)
The Consumer Price Index (CPI) rose from 134.96 in February 2025
to 137.14 in August 2025. The Bank of Uganda projects the inflation
to remain below the medium-term target of 5% during 2025/26.
Inflation adjustments apply to the local currency portion of O&M
costs for UEGCL (Nalubaale and Kiira), UETCL, and UEDCL, based
on approved local currency content: 71% for UEGCL, 72% for
UETCL, and 80% for UEDCL.
